title: Decision Trees & Ensembles
description: From a single tree's simple yes/no questions to the powerful ensembles — random forests and gradient boosting — built from many of them.

lessons.title: Decision Trees
lessons.description: Learn how a model can make predictions by asking a series of yes/no questions.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain how a decision tree makes predictions and why it's prone to overfitting on its own.

sections.title: 🌳 The core idea
sections.content:
A **decision tree** predicts by asking a sequence of simple yes/no questions about the features, splitting the data at each step, until it reaches a final prediction.

```
Is square_feet > 1500?
├── Yes → Is bedrooms > 3?
│         ├── Yes → predict $450,000
│         └── No  → predict $380,000
└── No  → predict $220,000
```

Each question is chosen (during training) to best separate the data into more "pure" groups — groups that share a more similar outcome.

sections.title: 🌱 How a tree is trained
sections.content:
```python
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

predictions = model.predict(X_test)
```

At each step, the algorithm picks the feature and threshold that best separates the classes (using a measure like Gini impurity or information gain) — repeating this recursively builds the full tree.

sections.title: ✅ Strengths and a big weakness
sections.content:
• **Easy to interpret** — you can literally read off the sequence of questions that led to a prediction
• **No feature scaling needed** — trees split on raw thresholds, unaffected by the units of measurement
• **Prone to overfitting** — an unconstrained tree can keep splitting until every training example gets its own leaf, perfectly memorizing the training data (and generalizing poorly)

Controlling tree depth (`max_depth`) or requiring a minimum number of samples per leaf are common ways to keep a tree from overfitting.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Letting a tree grow without any depth limit.** An unconstrained tree will often overfit dramatically — always set `max_depth` or another stopping rule.

**Judging a tree only by training accuracy.** A deep, unconstrained tree can hit near-100% training accuracy while performing badly on new data — the classic overfitting trap.

**Assuming a single decision tree is production-grade.** In practice, single trees are usually a stepping stone to the ensemble methods covered next — they rarely outperform ensembles on their own.

questions.question: How does a decision tree make a prediction?
options: By computing a weighted sum of all features at once
By following a sequence of yes/no questions about the features down to a final leaf prediction
By measuring distance to the nearest training examples
By clustering similar examples together
questions.explanation: A decision tree splits the data step by step based on feature thresholds, following a path of questions down to a leaf node that holds the final prediction.

questions.question: Why is an unconstrained decision tree prone to overfitting?
options: Trees can't actually be trained on real data
It can keep splitting until every training example has its own leaf, memorizing the training data rather than learning general patterns
Trees ignore the training data entirely
It's not actually prone to overfitting
questions.explanation: Without a depth limit or similar constraint, a tree can create extremely specific splits tailored to individual training examples — fitting the training data perfectly while failing to generalize.

questions.question: What's a common way to prevent a decision tree from overfitting?
options: Removing all training data
Limiting the tree's depth or requiring a minimum number of samples per leaf
Increasing the learning rate
Using more decimal places in calculations
questions.explanation: Constraining how deep the tree can grow, or how few samples a leaf can represent, keeps it from creating overly specific splits that memorize training data noise.

questions.question: What is a 'leaf' node in a decision tree?
options: The very first question asked at the top of the tree
A terminal node at the end of a path that gives the final prediction
A node that always splits into exactly two more nodes
A synonym for the tree's root node
questions.explanation: A leaf is where the decision path ends and the tree outputs its final prediction, with no further splits beneath it.

questions.question: How does a decision tree decide which feature to split on at each step?
options: It always splits on the first feature in the dataset
It chooses the split that most effectively separates the data into purer groups, using a measure like Gini impurity or information gain
It picks a feature at random every time
It splits on every feature simultaneously
questions.explanation: At each node, a decision tree evaluates possible splits and picks the one that best improves the purity of the resulting groups, using metrics like Gini impurity.

questions.question: What's an advantage of decision trees in terms of interpretability?
options: They are always black boxes with no interpretability at all
The decision path from root to leaf can be read as a clear sequence of understandable yes/no rules
They can only be interpreted by expert statisticians
Interpretability is not a relevant property for decision trees
questions.explanation: A key appeal of decision trees is that you can trace the exact sequence of feature comparisons that led to any given prediction.

questions.question: What does 'pruning' a decision tree mean?
options: Adding more branches to increase depth
Removing branches that add little predictive value, to reduce overfitting and simplify the tree
Deleting the entire tree and starting over
Doubling the amount of training data used
questions.explanation: Pruning trims back parts of a tree that don't meaningfully improve performance, helping control overfitting and producing a simpler, more generalizable tree.

questions.question: Why can decision trees handle both numeric and categorical features relatively naturally?
options: They can only handle one type of feature at a time
Splits can be formed as thresholds for numeric features or category membership checks for categorical ones, both fitting the same yes/no question structure
Categorical features must always be dropped before using a tree
Decision trees convert every feature into text before splitting
questions.explanation: The yes/no question structure of a tree split adapts naturally to both numeric thresholds (like age > 30) and categorical checks (like city == 'X').

lessons.title: Random Forests
lessons.description: Learn how combining many imperfect trees creates a much stronger, more reliable model.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain how a random forest works and why averaging many trees reduces overfitting.

sections.title: 🌲🌲🌲 The core idea: wisdom of the crowd
sections.content: A single decision tree overfits easily. A **random forest** trains *many* different decision trees and averages their predictions (for regression) or takes a majority vote (for classification). Individually noisy, imperfect trees combine into a much more stable, accurate model.

sections.title: 🎲 Two sources of randomness
sections.content:
Each tree in the forest is trained slightly differently, on purpose, so they make different kinds of mistakes:

• **Bagging (bootstrap aggregating)** — each tree trains on a random sample of the training data (drawn with replacement), so no two trees see quite the same data
• **Random feature selection** — at each split, each tree only considers a random subset of features, not all of them

This deliberate diversity is what makes averaging the trees' predictions so effective — errors that are somewhat random and uncorrelated tend to cancel out when combined.

sections.title: 🛠️ Using a random forest
sections.content:
```python
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

predictions = model.predict(X_test)
print(model.feature_importances_)  # which features mattered most, on average
```

• `n_estimators` — how many trees to build (more generally helps, up to diminishing returns)
• Random forests are far more resistant to overfitting than a single unconstrained tree
• A tradeoff: harder to interpret than a single tree — you can't easily "read off" one clean decision path anymore

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming more trees always keeps improving performance indefinitely.** Gains taper off — at some point, adding more trees mostly costs computation time without meaningfully improving accuracy.

**Losing the interpretability advantage without realizing it.** A forest of 100 trees can't be "read" the way a single small tree can — use `feature_importances_` for interpretability instead of trying to trace individual trees.

**Forgetting that random forests still need a validation set.** They're more overfitting-resistant than a single tree, but they aren't immune, especially on small or noisy datasets.

questions.question: What's the core idea behind a random forest?
options: Training one very large, very deep tree
Training many different decision trees and combining their predictions, which reduces overfitting compared to any single tree
Removing decision trees in favor of a single linear model
Using only the single best-performing tree out of many candidates
questions.explanation: A random forest builds an ensemble of many trees, each trained slightly differently, and combines their predictions — this averaging cancels out much of the overfitting any individual tree would show on its own.

questions.question: What are the two main sources of randomness that make trees in a forest diverse?
options: Different programming languages and different computers
Bootstrap-sampled training data per tree, and a random subset of features considered at each split
Randomly shuffling the final predictions
Random initial weights, like in a neural network
questions.explanation: Each tree sees a random sample of the training rows (bagging) and considers only a random subset of features at each split — both introduce controlled diversity that makes averaging the trees' predictions effective.

questions.question: What's a tradeoff of using a random forest compared to a single decision tree?
options: Random forests always perform worse
Random forests are harder to interpret — you can't trace one clean decision path the way you can with a single small tree
Random forests can't be used for classification
Random forests never overfit under any circumstances
questions.explanation: The averaging that makes forests more accurate and stable also makes them less directly interpretable than a single tree — you generally rely on aggregate feature importance rather than tracing individual decision paths.

questions.question: How does a random forest combine the predictions of its individual trees for a classification task?
options: It picks the single tree with the highest confidence
It typically takes a majority vote across all the trees' individual predictions
It averages every tree's raw training data
It selects one tree at random each time
questions.explanation: For classification, a random forest commonly aggregates predictions from its trees using majority voting to reach a final decision.

questions.question: What does 'bootstrap sampling' mean in the context of building a random forest?
options: Using the exact same full dataset for every tree
Sampling the training data with replacement to create a slightly different training set for each tree
Sampling only categorical features
Deleting rows to shrink the dataset before training
questions.explanation: Bootstrap sampling draws random samples with replacement from the training data, giving each tree in the forest a slightly different (but overlapping) training set.

questions.question: Why does averaging or voting across many diverse trees tend to reduce overfitting compared to a single deep tree?
options: It doesn't — averaging trees always overfits more
Individual trees' errors tend to be somewhat independent, so combining them cancels out much of each tree's individual noise
Averaging removes the need for any training data
Random forests use fewer training examples per tree, which alone prevents overfitting
questions.explanation: Because each tree tends to make somewhat different mistakes, combining many trees' predictions averages out a lot of the individual noise, improving generalization.

questions.question: What is 'feature importance' in a random forest typically based on?
options: The alphabetical order of feature names
How much each feature contributes to reducing impurity across the splits it's used in, aggregated across all trees
A random assignment with no basis in the data
Only the very first split in the very first tree
questions.explanation: Feature importance is usually computed by measuring how much each feature contributes to improving split quality (like reducing impurity) across all trees in the forest.

questions.question: Why might you still choose a single decision tree over a random forest in some situations?
options: Single trees are always more accurate than forests
When interpretability of the exact decision path matters more than squeezing out maximum predictive accuracy
Single decision trees train slower than random forests in every case
There's never a good reason to prefer a single tree
questions.explanation: If being able to explain the exact reasoning behind a prediction matters more than raw performance, a single interpretable tree can be preferable to an ensemble.

lessons.title: Gradient Boosting
lessons.description: Learn how building trees one at a time, each fixing the last one's mistakes, produces some of the strongest tabular-data models around.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain the core idea behind gradient boosting and how it differs from a random forest.

sections.title: 🎯 A different ensemble strategy
sections.content:
Random forests build many trees *independently* and average them. **Gradient boosting** builds trees *sequentially* — each new tree is trained specifically to correct the mistakes (the residual errors) of the trees built so far.

• Random forest: many independent trees, averaged (reduces variance)
• Gradient boosting: trees built one after another, each fixing prior errors (reduces bias, gradually)

sections.title: 🔁 The step-by-step idea
sections.content:
1. Start with a simple initial prediction (like the average target value)
2. Compute the errors (residuals) between predictions and actual values
3. Train a new small tree to predict those *errors*
4. Add a scaled-down version of that tree's predictions to the running total
5. Repeat for many rounds, gradually reducing the remaining error

Each individual tree is usually shallow and weak on its own — the power comes from combining many of them, each nudging the prediction a little closer to correct.

sections.title: 🛠️ Popular implementations
sections.content:
```python
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier

model = GradientBoostingClassifier(
    n_estimators=200,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_depth=3,
)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
```

In practice, most real-world tabular ML competitions and production systems use faster, more optimized boosting libraries like **XGBoost**, **LightGBM**, or **CatBoost**, which follow the same core idea with engineering improvements.

• `learning_rate` — how much each new tree's correction counts; smaller values need more trees but often generalize better
• `n_estimators` — how many rounds of boosting to run
• Gradient boosting is often the strongest "off-the-shelf" choice for structured/tabular data

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Setting the learning rate and number of trees independently without considering both together.** A low learning rate typically needs more trees to compensate — they're tuned as a pair, not separately.

**Not watching for overfitting.** Because each tree targets the remaining error, boosting can eventually start fitting noise if allowed to run for too many rounds — validation-set monitoring (and early stopping) helps catch this.

**Assuming boosting is always better than a random forest.** It's frequently stronger, but it's also more sensitive to hyperparameter tuning and can be slower to train — a forest is a very reasonable first baseline.

questions.question: How does gradient boosting differ from a random forest in how trees are built?
options: Boosting builds trees independently; forests build them sequentially
Boosting builds trees sequentially, each correcting the errors of the ones before it; a forest builds trees independently and averages them
There is no real difference between the two methods
Boosting only uses a single tree total
questions.explanation: Random forests average many independently-trained trees; gradient boosting builds trees one at a time, each specifically targeting the remaining errors of the combined trees so far.

questions.question: What does each new tree in a gradient boosting model typically try to predict?
options: The original target value from scratch
The remaining errors (residuals) left by the trees built so far
A completely random target
The feature importances of the previous tree
questions.explanation: Each new tree is trained to predict the current residual error, and its (scaled) prediction is added to the running total — gradually reducing the overall error round by round.

questions.question: Why are the learning rate and number of trees usually tuned together in gradient boosting?
options: They have no relationship to each other
A smaller learning rate means each tree contributes less, so more trees (rounds) are typically needed to reach good performance
Learning rate only matters for random forests
The number of trees is fixed and can't be changed
questions.explanation: Learning rate controls how much each tree's correction counts toward the final prediction — a smaller rate needs more rounds (trees) to compensate, so the two settings are tuned as a pair rather than independently.

questions.question: Why is gradient boosting generally more sensitive to overfitting than a random forest, if not carefully tuned?
options: It isn't — boosting is always less prone to overfitting
Because each tree is fit specifically to correct the errors of the previous ones, too many rounds can start fitting noise in the training data
Boosting doesn't use decision trees at all
Random forests are never at risk of overfitting
questions.explanation: Since boosting keeps chasing the remaining errors round after round, without proper tuning (like limiting rounds or learning rate) it can start fitting noise rather than signal.

questions.question: What role does the learning rate play in gradient boosting?
options: It controls how many features are used per tree
It scales down how much each new tree's correction contributes to the overall prediction, trading speed for stability
It has no effect on the model's training
It determines the maximum depth of each tree
questions.explanation: A smaller learning rate shrinks each tree's contribution, generally leading to more stable, better-generalizing models at the cost of needing more trees.

questions.question: What is a well-known gradient boosting implementation commonly used in practice?
options: K-means
XGBoost (or similar libraries like LightGBM)
Linear regression
K-nearest neighbors
questions.explanation: XGBoost and similar libraries like LightGBM are popular, optimized implementations of gradient boosting widely used for tabular data problems.

questions.question: Why is gradient boosting often a strong choice for structured, tabular data competitions?
options: It requires no hyperparameter tuning at all
It tends to achieve high predictive accuracy on tabular data by effectively correcting successive rounds of errors
It's the only algorithm capable of handling tabular data
It always trains faster than every other algorithm
questions.explanation: Gradient boosting's ability to iteratively refine predictions often makes it one of the most accurate approaches for structured tabular datasets.

questions.question: What happens to the training process if the learning rate in gradient boosting is set very high?
options: Training becomes perfectly stable regardless of other settings
Each tree's correction has an outsized effect, which can cause the model to overshoot and perform poorly, similar to a too-large learning rate in gradient descent
The number of trees needed increases dramatically
It has no meaningful effect on training
questions.explanation: Just like in general gradient descent, too large a learning rate can cause updates (here, tree contributions) to overshoot and destabilize training.

lessons.title: Bagging vs. Boosting: A Recap
lessons.description: Consolidate the difference between these two ensemble strategies with a clear side-by-side comparison.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can clearly compare bagging and boosting and know when each is a natural fit.

sections.title: 🧩 Two ways to combine weak learners
sections.content:
Both bagging (random forests) and boosting (gradient boosting) combine many individual trees into one stronger model — but they combine them in fundamentally different ways.

• **Bagging** — trees trained independently and in parallel, on random samples of the data, then averaged
• **Boosting** — trees trained sequentially, each one correcting the errors of the trees before it

sections.title: ⚖️ What each is good at
sections.content:
• Bagging (random forests) primarily reduces **variance** — it's great at stabilizing an already-decent model that's overfitting due to being too sensitive to its specific training sample
• Boosting primarily reduces **bias** — it's great at gradually improving a model that's systematically missing patterns, by continually chasing the remaining error

In practice, both are strong choices for tabular data, and boosting (especially XGBoost/LightGBM) often edges out forests on raw accuracy — at the cost of being more sensitive to hyperparameter tuning and slightly more prone to overfitting if not carefully monitored.

sections.title: 🛠️ Practical guidance
sections.content:
• **Start with a random forest** as a strong, relatively low-effort baseline — it's fairly robust to default settings
• **Reach for gradient boosting** (or XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost) when you have time to tune it and want to squeeze out more accuracy
• Both are typically far stronger than a single decision tree, and both remain highly competitive choices for structured/tabular data — even in a world of deep learning

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming one ensemble method is always strictly better than the other.** It depends on the dataset and how much tuning effort you can invest — trying both is often worthwhile.

**Forgetting both methods still need a held-out validation or test set.** Ensembles reduce overfitting risk but don't eliminate the need for honest evaluation.

**Jumping straight to boosting without trying a simpler baseline first.** A random forest (or even plain logistic/linear regression) is a fast, useful sanity check before investing in a more complex, tunable model.

questions.question: What's the key structural difference between bagging and boosting?
options: Bagging uses neural networks; boosting uses trees
Bagging trains trees independently in parallel; boosting trains trees sequentially, each correcting prior errors
They are identical techniques with different names
Bagging can only be used for regression
questions.explanation: Bagging (as in random forests) builds many trees independently and averages them; boosting builds trees one after another, each specifically targeting the errors left by the previous ones.

questions.question: Which type of error does boosting primarily target?
options: Variance, by averaging many independent models
Bias, by sequentially correcting the errors the combined model has made so far
Neither — boosting doesn't affect bias or variance
Only errors in categorical features
questions.explanation: Boosting continually chases whatever error remains after the trees built so far — this sequential error-correction process primarily works to reduce bias (systematic underfitting).

questions.question: What's a sensible default strategy when starting a new tabular ML problem?
options: Jump straight to the most complex boosting setup available
Start with a simple baseline like a random forest, then consider gradient boosting if more accuracy is needed and tuning time is available
Only ever use a single decision tree
Skip evaluation entirely and deploy the first model trained
questions.explanation: A random forest is a strong, relatively low-effort baseline; boosting methods can often improve on that but cost more tuning effort — starting simple and escalating only if needed is a practical approach.

questions.question: How does bagging primarily reduce error?
options: By reducing bias through sequential error correction
By reducing variance, since averaging many independently trained models smooths out individual model noise
By eliminating the need for a validation set
Bagging doesn't reduce any type of error
questions.explanation: Bagging's main benefit comes from reducing variance — averaging independent models' predictions cancels out much of each individual model's noise.

questions.question: Can bagging and boosting both be applied using decision trees as the base model?
options: No, boosting can only be used with linear models
Yes — random forests use bagging with trees, and gradient boosting uses boosting with trees
No, bagging can only be used with neural networks
Only bagging can use decision trees as a base model
questions.explanation: Both major ensemble strategies commonly use decision trees as their base learners — random forests apply bagging, while gradient boosting applies boosting.

questions.question: Why does boosting typically train its models sequentially rather than in parallel like bagging?
options: Sequential training is purely a historical convention with no technical reason
Each new model in boosting needs to know the errors made by the previous models, which requires those earlier models to already be trained
Sequential training is actually faster than parallel training
Boosting doesn't actually use multiple models
questions.explanation: Because each boosting round is specifically designed to correct the mistakes of the ensemble so far, it inherently depends on knowing what those prior mistakes were.

questions.question: What's a reasonable approach if a random forest baseline isn't accurate enough for a project's needs?
options: Immediately abandon tree-based methods entirely
Try gradient boosting with careful tuning, since it often squeezes out additional accuracy at the cost of more careful tuning
Reduce the dataset size to make the problem easier
Switch to using no model at all
questions.explanation: When a simple ensemble baseline isn't sufficient, gradient boosting is a natural next step, often improving accuracy in exchange for more careful hyperparameter tuning.

questions.question: Why is starting with a simple ensemble baseline generally good practice before jumping to advanced tuning?
options: It's not good practice — always start with the most complex model available
It establishes a solid reference point and quickly reveals whether a simpler model is already good enough for the task
Simple baselines are required by every ML library
It skips the need for any further evaluation
questions.explanation: A quick, simple baseline shows whether the problem is already reasonably solved and gives a fair benchmark to judge whether additional complexity is actually worth the effort.
